World.title: Heat record broken again, Hungary one of the hottest countries in Europe
World.content:
Hungary was one of the hottest countries in Europe on Monday, with maximum temperatures mostly ranging between 36 and 40 degrees Celsius. Yesterday the temperature in southern Budapest dropped to just 26.8 degrees Celsius at dawn, which is another heat record.

Heat records broken on Monday

On 3 August, the temperature in southern Budapest dropped to just 26.8 degrees Celsius at dawn, surpassing the previous national record of 25.1C, measured in 2017, weather service HungaroMet reported on Tuesday.

In the afternoon, 39.6C was registered in northern Budapest, breaking the previous record of 38.7C measured in 2017.

Sweltering heatwave in Hungary. Photo: Anadolu/Németi Róbert

Hungary one of hottest countries in Europe on Monday

Hungary was one of the hottest countries in Europe on Monday, with maximum temperatures mostly ranging between 36 and 40 degrees Celsius, and the daily average temperatures typically stood between 27C and 30C, weather service HungaroMet said on Facebook.

Europe continues to be characterised by hot weather, with maximum temperatures exceeding 30C across much of the continent.

Photo: Anadolu/Németi Róbert

If you missed: Heatwave peaking: could the record temperature be broken? Latest forecast

The cold front that passed north of Hungary two days ago temporarily helped ease the heat in Germany, Poland and Northern Europe, the service said.

Dunamenti Power Plant operating safely, minister says

The Dunamenti Power Plant is operating safely and the last turbine of the Paks nuclear power plant is still operating, Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány said on Facebook on Tuesday. “Imports are secured and consumption is lower as a result of the cooperation,” Kapitány said.

World.title: The aluminium cans gain ground in Romania: its share of DRS packaging has risen to 29.3%
World.content:
News from Companies

Official RetuRO data analysed by Every Can Counts shows an increase from 21.6% in the first quarter of 2024 to 29.3% in the second quarter of 2026. One driver of this growth is the younger generation, drawn to the graphic freedom the can offers and to its infinite recyclability.

Since the launch of the Deposit Return System at the end of 2023, the aluminium can has risen visibly within Romania's beverage packaging mix. According to official RetuRO reports, metal's share of all DRS packaging placed on the market grew from 21.6% in the first quarter of 2024 to 29.3% in the second quarter of 2026. The same trend appears in returns, where metal reached 28.8%, up from 18.7% at the start of the system.



That is an increase of almost eight percentage points in two years, in a market where plastic remains dominant but is declining: from 61% to 51% of volumes placed on the market over the same period. Glass has held steady, at around 20%.

Metal rises quarter after quarter



The can's share has grown steadily since 2024, peaking in the second quarter of 2026, which points to a structural trend. The explanation lies in several overlapping factors: the widening range of beverages sold in cans, a clearer consumer preference for lightweight, portable packaging, and a context in which aluminium is becoming the material of choice for brands building their identity around sustainability.



The trend also holds internationally. According to an April 2026 McKinsey analysis, the metal packaging segment continued to show steady volume growth, and in certain categories metal is gaining market share thanks to portability, recyclability, and premiumisation trends.



The aluminium can is recycled indefinitely, with no loss of quality, and can return to the shelf in as little as 60 days. Every recycled can saves up to 95% of the energy needed to produce a new one from raw materials.

The can as a space for brand expression



The can's rise also has a cultural dimension, most visible among younger consumers. The surface of the can works as a continuous canvas, with no separate label and no interruptions, giving designers a creative space that other packaging materials cannot match. Today's metal printing technologies allow intense colours, matte finishes, phosphorescent inks, and limited editions, and producers offer dozens of sizes and decoration techniques for brands looking to stand out on the shelf.



For young consumers, packaging has become an extension of personal style. An article published by Ad Age in 2024 found that 81% of Gen Z consumers have tried a product because of its packaging, and 63% repeated the purchase for the same reason. The same generation sees metal as the most environmentally responsible choice, according to 2024 McKinsey research indicating that 60% of young people prefer recyclable packaging. Across Europe, a study conducted by the agency Caramel for Sonoco found that 82% of consumers are more likely to buy a product that comes in metal packaging.



These preferences explain why more and more beverage brands are choosing the can: on the shelf, it becomes part of how they are recognised.

Romanians want recycling to become an experience



The Deposit Return System built the habit of recycling quickly. Romania's national recycling rate for aluminium cans reached 75% in 2025, more than double the level of 2022, when European Commission data indicated just 35%. Yet the Every Can Counts Global Study 2025, based on a sample of more than 16,000 participants across 16 countries, including 1,013 in Romania, shows that Romanians want more from the act of recycling.



Three in four Romanians (75%) say they would recycle more if the experience were more enjoyable or more interactive, through rewards, games, or apps that track and celebrate recycling. At the same time, Romanians are among the most engaged consumers in the world: 71% feel personally responsible for recycling, the highest figure globally, and 91% believe producers should be required to use packaging that is fully recyclable or made from recycled materials.



The data points to a market ready for more than automated collection: Romanians want more accessible return points (38%) and a faster process (41%), but above all an experience that gives the gesture meaning.

"The fact that more and more brands are choosing the aluminium can is good news for circularity. It is a packaging that is infinitely recyclable and already collected at scale, which means that every can recycled can become another can, in as little as 60 days. When people see how quickly the loop closes, recycling becomes a gesture with meaning. That is what we set out to do at Every Can Counts: to bring circularity closer to people, so that every can truly counts." said David Van Heuverswyn, Global Director of Every Can Counts.

From the shelf to an art installation



Every Can Counts Romania responds directly to this need through visible projects and interactive activations with the public. The "I CAN" installations, made entirely from aluminium cans by Romanian artist Sergiu Chihaia, turn recycling into an experience people can see and touch. Through campaigns and public art projects, the programme brings circularity closer to people and gives an everyday gesture a moment of cultural impact.



Counties with strong sustainability initiatives, such as Bucharest, Timiș, Cluj, Ilfov, and Constanța, lead the national rankings for recycling rates.

Data sources: RetuRO; the Every Can Counts Global Recycling Habits and Attitudes 2025 study; Ad Age, 2024; McKinsey research, 2024; the McKinsey analysis "No ordinary disruption: State of the packaging and paper industry," April 2026; and the Caramel study for Sonoco.



*This is a press release.

World.title: Romanian PM says no fuel supply problems expected as energy system remains under pressure
World.content:
Romanian authorities do not currently expect problems with fuel supplies for households, agriculture, or transport companies, interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan said on Tuesday, August 4. His comments came after three government meetings on the country's energy situation, fuel supplies, and measures to maintain the stability of the national power system.

Ilie Bolojan, who is also the acting minister of energy, said the situation had improved, with the OMV refinery processing at full capacity and Petromidia operating at around 85% of capacity. The latter is expected to return to normal operations by the end of the week.

“At this moment, we do not anticipate problems regarding fuel supplies for the population, agriculture and transport operators," Bolojan said.

The assurances come amid a sharp rise in fuel prices. Diesel has climbed above RON 10.80 per liter in Bucharest after more than a week of sustained increases, while gasoline is selling for more than RON 9.50 per liter at some filling stations, Euronews Romania reported. According to the broadcaster, Romania recorded the highest increase in fuel prices in the European Union over the past week, at 7.5%, adding around RON 57 to the cost of a full tank.

In this context, president Nicușor Dan announced on Tuesday that he had signed the decree promulgating legislation introducing measures aimed at stabilizing the petroleum products market amid rising fuel prices.

"Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and extreme volatility on the international oil market have generated rapid increases in fuel prices, including in our country," Dan said. "Rapid state intervention was once again necessary because these price increases translate into higher costs throughout the economy for citizens and businesses, with direct effects on purchasing power, economic competitiveness, and the stability of critical national sectors."

According to the president, the legislation provides for declaring a crisis situation on the petroleum products market, reducing the excise duty on diesel, capping commercial markups, and temporarily banning diesel exports without prior approval from the Energy Ministry in order to prioritize domestic consumption. It also introduces a solidarity contribution for large oil companies.

The government also reviewed the situation at the Cernavodă nuclear power plant amid low Danube levels. Dredging and rock removal works are continuing, while an operation involving the sinking of barges is planned once all technical conditions are met.

The measures are intended to extend the operation of Unit 2 for as long as possible, according to the prime minister.

“The water level at Cernavodă has not fallen further. This is a good sign, but the situation remains difficult, and we are continuing all measures to keep the unit operating for as long as possible," Bolojan said. "Every day of operation means additional energy for the National Energy System.”

The prime minister also met with major electricity suppliers to discuss measures aimed at maintaining balance in the energy system. The talks covered ways of ensuring market liquidity through the payment of outstanding amounts under the compensation scheme, as well as cooperation with grid operator Transelectrica on voluntary reductions in electricity consumption by large industrial consumers.

The government also agreed with energy regulator ANRE to accelerate the issuance of documents required for projects already at an advanced stage, allowing new power generation capacity to come online as quickly as possible.

At the same time, the government is preparing a backup mechanism that could temporarily limit electricity consumption by major industrial users if voluntary reductions prove insufficient during peak hours.

“In the coming days, we will adopt a government decision implementing the mechanism provided by law for situations in which voluntary consumption reductions are not sufficient to cover electricity demand during peak hours," Ilie Bolojan said.

Under the mechanism, large consumers could receive 24 hours' notice of temporary consumption limits, depending on the nature of their operations and the capacity of the National Energy System.

World.title: DP World pilots Western Europe-Romania rail route for finished vehicles, with Aiud as regional distribution hub
World.content:
DP World announced that it completed its first delivery of finished vehicles by rail from Zeebrugge in Belgium to Aiud, Romania, launching a new intermodal corridor between Western and Southeastern Europe. The company plans to develop Aiud into a regional distribution hub for finished vehicles serving Romania and neighboring markets.

The initial shipment is destined for Chișinău, Moldova, with the vehicles continuing their journey by road from Aiud. According to DP World, it is the company's first vehicle rail operation in Europe managed end-to-end.

Following the pilot, DP World plans to introduce a regular service with twice-monthly operations during the second half of 2026. The company also plans to establish similar connections between Aiud and other European ports, including Koper in Slovenia.

“Automotive companies are looking to reduce their exposure to long-distance road transport. By combining rail and road in a single integrated service, we are giving customers greater reliability, lower emissions and a solution that can scale as trade flows across Europe continue to evolve,” said Dragoș Călin, Director Freight, Balkans at DP World.

The company estimates that using the intermodal rail and road service can reduce CO2 emissions by up to 55% compared with equivalent long-haul road transport. It said the service could also provide greater cost certainty and predictability by reducing exposure to changing European road transport regulations, road usage charges, and cross-border administrative procedures.

“Our strategy is to build a more connected European logistics network, creating new trade corridors and giving customers greater choice in how they move goods across the continent," said DP World Romania CEO Svitlana Balaban. "Aiud is an important part of that vision, creating new links between western European ports and markets across southeastern Europe.”

DP World's multimodal logistics terminal in Aiud opened in 2024 following a EUR 21 million investment. The 180,000 sqm facility is located next to the A10 motorway and connected to Romania's national rail network, providing container handling, storage, customs and freight forwarding services.

World.title: Haferland Week kicks off in ten historic villages in Transylvania
World.content:
The 14th edition of Haferland Week, a festival celebrating the culture and traditions of Transylvanian Saxons, will open on Thursday, August 6, in ten historic villages in Haferland (the Land of Oats), namely Archita, Viscri, Cloașterf, Bunești, Meșendorf, Rupea, Saschiz, Roadeș, Criț and Homorod.

The opening of the event, set to take place in the square in front of the fortified church in Archita, will be followed by a brass band concert by Original Karpaten-Express, performances of traditional Saxon folk dances, children's theatre, and cultural activities for all ages, including traditional crafts workshops.

Among this year's highlights are a concert in Cloașterf featuring songs from the repertoire of Romanian folk icon Maria Tănase, reinterpreted by Luiza Zan & Jazzpar Trio, and a jazz evening in Rupea with Luiza Zan, Mariano Castro & Muse Quartet. The program also includes performances of traditional Saxon music by Original Karpaten-Express Kulturwerk der Siebenbürger Sachsen and Siebenbürger Trachtenkapelle Göppingen.

The festival will also feature brass band concerts and parades, traditional dances, and guided tours of the region's fortified churches. One of the highlights will be the hike to the refuge fortress of Saschiz, accompanied by surprise musical performances along the route and culminating in a cultural picnic on the fortress grounds. The fortified church in Saschiz is one of two in Haferland listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, alongside the fortified church in Viscri.

The program includes around 60 events, ranging from theatre performances for children and adults to traditional craft workshops, including furniture painting, embroidery, basket weaving, felting, making traditional bags and baskets, and postcard writing, among many others.

Visitors to Criț during the festival's final two days will also have the opportunity to see Agapi – Half a Century of Love, an exhibition by Kira Hagi. On Saturday, August 8, the barn of the fortified church in Criț will host one of Haferland Week's most anticipated events: a parade of three traditional Saxon music ensembles, followed by a traditional Saxon ball accompanied by the German-based Saxon band Flamingo Sound Nürnberg.

On the festival's closing day, following the official ceremony and speeches by guests, audiences will be shown the teaser for the documentary Nadia. The Perfect Ten. The screening will take place in the presence of Nadia Comăneci, the legendary Romanian gymnast who became the first athlete in Olympic history to receive a perfect 10 at the 1976 Montreal Olympics.

(Photo: Fortified church in Criț by Calin Stan | Dreamstime.com)

World.title: Bucharest International Ballet Gala to bring Swan Lake to Sala Palatului in March 2027
World.content:
The Bucharest International Ballet Gala will return for its second edition on March 30, 2027, with a production of Swan Lake featuring internationally renowned ballet dancers Iana Salenko and Daniil Simkin. The performance, presented by the Sibiu Ballet Theatre, will take place at Sala Palatului.

The event will mark the first time Salenko and Simkin perform together on a Romanian stage, according to the organizers.

Iana Salenko will take on the dual role of Odette/Odile, while Daniil Simkin will perform as Prince Siegfried in the classical ballet set to Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's score.

They will be joined by dancers from the Sibiu Ballet Theatre, led by director Ovidiu Dragoman. The production will feature classical choreography alongside sets and costumes created for the performance.

Swan Lake tells the story of Prince Siegfried and Princess Odette, who has been transformed into a swan by a sorcerer's curse. It is one of the best-known works in the classical ballet repertoire.

Tickets for the Bucharest performance are available through Ticketstore, iabilet.ro and the Sala Palatului box office.

World.title: Bucharest hospital Ponderas puts EUR 1.7 mln in hybrid angiography and cardiovascular surgery suite
World.content:
Ponderas Academic Hospital, part of the network of private healthcare provider Regina Maria, has opened a hybrid operating suite for the diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular diseases following a EUR 1.7 million investment.

The suite “enables interventional radiology procedures and image-guided, minimally invasive treatments, strengthening the hospital's capacity to manage complex cardiovascular surgery and interventional cardiology cases simultaneously,” it said.

"The hybrid suite changes the options available to us when treating complex cardiovascular cases. Its main advantage is that it allows us to do more for patients in a less invasive way. Procedures that previously had to be performed in separate stages, requiring two hospital admissions and two rounds of anesthesia, can now be carried out during a single intervention. For patients, this means less time in hospital and an easier recovery," Dr. Cătălin Trifan, attending cardiovascular surgeon at Ponderas Academic Hospital, said.

The hospital has nearly 400 inpatient beds, 38 day-care beds, 43 intensive care beds and 14 operating theatres. It also has three dedicated emergency departments: for adults, pediatrics, and obstetrics and gynecology.

The hospital was established in 2010 as a center dedicated to bariatric and metabolic surgery. After its integration into the Regina Maria network in 2016, it expanded the range of medical specialties. Over the past few years, investments have exceeded EUR 20 million, helping to double the hospital's capacity while supporting annual growth in activity of more than 10%.

(Photo: the company)

World.title: Exhibition on historic Saxon dress of southern Transylvania at fortified church in Cincșor
World.content:
Wearing Transylvania: Saxon Presence, an exhibition exploring the historic Saxon costume as a reflection of the culture that shaped southern Transylvania for centuries, will open at the fortified church in Cincșor this weekend.

The exhibition brings together late 19th- and early 20th-century Saxon costumes, archival and contemporary photography, and reproductions of paintings from the European Art Gallery of the Brukenthal National Museum.

“Historic costume belongs as much to the places where it was worn as it does to museum collections. This idea lies at the heart of Wearing Transylvania, a series of exhibitions dedicated to the research, preservation and reinterpretation of Transylvania's textile heritage. Each chapter explores the material culture of a particular community and its relationship with the landscape it shaped, inhabited and gave its identity,” a presentation of the exhibition reads.

The exhibition was conceived and curated by architect Ana Maria Crișan. It includes historic Saxon costumes from the Drăgaica Roșie Collection of traditional costumes and textiles, documented in collaboration with Sebastian Paic-Apan, curator at the Transylvanian Ethnographic Museum in Cluj-Napoca, photographic projections by architect Alexandru Crișan, and reproductions of paintings from the European Art Gallery of the Brukenthal National Museum.

The program of the opening day also includes a seasonal brunch with local specialties, served in the garden of the former Evangelical parish house, organized in partnership with the My Transylvania Association; and a guided tour and quiz for children at the fortified church in Cincșor.

The exhibition, organized by the Culture Reserve Association and the Contrafort Pro Kleinschenk/Cincșor Association, will be on view from August 8 to October 1.

(All photos: the organizers)

World.title: Extreme heat expands across Romania, red alert extended in west with temperatures up to 41°C
World.content:
An intense heatwave will persist and expand across Romania through Thursday morning, August 6, with the highest red-level warning extended to seven western and northwestern counties and temperatures expected to reach 41°C. The rest of the country will be under orange and yellow heat alerts, according to updated warnings issued by the National Meteorological Administration (ANM).

On Tuesday, August 4, a red alert is in force for Satu Mare, Bihor, Arad, and Timiș counties, where temperatures will reach 38-40°C. Meteorologists said the extreme temperatures will be comparable to absolute records for August, while nighttime lows could remain as high as 24-26°C.

An orange alert covers Maramureș, southern Banat, most of Transylvania, northeastern Moldova, and southwestern Oltenia, with highs of 35-39°C. The rest of much of the country, including Muntenia, Dobrogea, most of Moldova, and Oltenia and eastern and southeastern Transylvania, is under a yellow alert, with temperatures generally reaching 31-38°C.

Photo: Meteoromania.ro

The heatwave will intensify further on Wednesday, August 5, when the red alert will expand to Maramureș, Satu Mare, Sălaj, Bihor, Arad, Timiș, and Caraș-Severin counties. Temperatures there will reach 37-39°C in Maramureș, Satu Mare, and Sălaj and 39-41°C in Bihor, Arad, Timiș, and Caraș-Severin.

Meanwhile, Moldova, Oltenia, most of Transylvania, and southwestern and central Muntenia, including Bucharest, will be under an orange alert on Wednesday, with highs of 35-38°C. A yellow warning will cover Dobrogea, northern and eastern Muntenia, and eastern Transylvania, where temperatures will reach up to 36-37°C.

Photo: Meteoromania.ro

Thermal discomfort will be high to extreme across large parts of the country, with the temperature-humidity index reaching or exceeding the critical threshold of 80. Tropical nights, with minimum temperatures of 20-26°C, are expected across most regions.

ANM said the heatwave would remain persistent and intensify across all regions on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. It is expected to weaken on Friday, August 7, and gradually retreat towards the southern half of the country.

Periods of atmospheric instability are also forecast. Torrential rain, thunderstorms, strong winds, squalls, and isolated hail are expected particularly in the Eastern Carpathians on Tuesday and Wednesday, across much of the mountain area on Thursday, and in northern Romania on Friday. Rainfall amounts could reach 10-25 liters per square meter over short periods of one to three hours.

The broader weather advisory covering the heatwave and atmospheric instability remains in effect until the morning of August 8, while ANM said it would update the warnings depending on the evolution and intensity of the weather.

World.title: Kosovo Detains Third Suspect as Mass Grave Probe Expands in North
World.content:
The Kosovo prosecution announced on Tuesday that investigations into the remains of missing persons from the Kosovo 1998-99 war are being conducted in a third location in the Serb-majority north of the country, as three persons suspected of war crimes have been detained.

“The Special Prosecution … confirms that, in coordination with the Kosovo Police, investigations regarding the war crimes case in the municipality of Zubin Potok are proceeding intensively.

“To date, three individuals have been arrested on suspicion of committing the criminal offence of ‘War crimes against the civilian population.’ Several locations have been searched during the investigations. Remains found in the village of Jabuke will undergo forensic examination and DNA analysis for identification purposes, while excavation work continues in the village of Kalluder e Vogel/Mala Kaludra. Currently, investigations are also underway at a third location,” the prosecution wrote on Facebook.

The Pristina Basic Court on Monday ordered one month’s pre-trial detention for a suspect identified only as J.R., who is under investigation for alleged war crimes against civilians and was arrested on August 2 in connection with the investigation. The court said there was a risk that the suspect, a Serbian citizen, “could flee to avoid prosecution … and could influence witnesses or evidence if released”.

“The measure of detention is necessary to ensure the defendant’s presence and the uninterrupted conduct of criminal proceedings,” the court said.

J.R. is the third person arrested in the case. Two other suspects, M.J. and M.B., were detained as excavation work began in the village of Kalluder e Vogel/Mala Kaludra on July 28. Both remain in custody.

The Special Prosecution has not given details on the specific allegations against the suspects but has said that their arrests are “related to the investigation into alleged war crimes against the civilian population” during the Kosovo war. The Prosecution said there is evidence that one of the suspects had been “mobilised and served actively in the former Yugoslav Army during the Kosovo war”.

Excavations at Kalluder e Vogel/Mala Kaludra began on July 28 after the Special Prosecution sought a court order to investigate a suspected mass grave containing victims of the war.

Acting Prime Minister Albin Kurti said these remains might belong to the so-called “group of intellectuals” – a group of Albanian civilians, including doctors, professors and lawyers, who disappeared on April 19, 1999. “We cannot confirm that they are the victims in question but that was our immediate suspicion. We must wait for our institutions to determine exactly what has been found there,” Kurti said on July 29.

On August 2, the Special Prosecution and police announced that investigators had identified a second suspected burial site in the nearby village of Jabuke, also in Zubin Potok municipality.

Late on Monday, the government’s Commission on Missing Persons said excavations had continued at both sites. “Because of the terrain, work focused on Jabuke, where the remains of four individuals were exhumed,” it said. adding that preliminary assessments indicate that the victims were likely people who were forcibly disappeared during the Kosovo war. “The remains have been transferred to the Institute of Forensic Medicine for examination and DNA identification,” the Commission said.

Acting Interior Minister Xhelal Svecla, who visited the site, said the “victims were thrown into a lime pit after being executed”.

While the investigation is continuing, there were reports that Serbian authorities had arrested a Kosovo citizen from Istog on suspicion of espionage. Kosovo officials have linked the arrest to the ongoing search for wartime mass graves.

Svecla accused Serbia of “refusing to provide information about people who disappeared during the war while intimidating those who cooperate with investigations.

“This state, on the one hand, refuses to provide information about forcibly disappeared persons, while on the other hand threatens and imprisons its own citizens who cooperate in locating these graves,” he said.

Acting Minister for Labour, Family, Social Welfare and War Veterans Andin Hoti described the reported arrest as “an attempted murder of the truth”, alleging that it was intended to discourage witnesses from assisting investigations into missing persons.

A report published on July 29 by Kosovo’s Institute of Crimes Committed During the War said 1,578 people remain missing from the 1998-99 Kosovo war.

World.title: Romania Cuts Industrial Output to Ease Power Shortage
World.content:
More than 80 of Romania’s largest energy-intensive companies, including car manufacturers, steel producers, fertilizer plants and other major industrial consumers, are to begin maintenance work or scale back production from Tuesday, to ease pressure on the national power grid.

The measures come as a prolonged heatwave drives electricity demand to seasonal highs while severe drought has sharply reduced hydropower generation and affected operations at Romania’s only nuclear power plant, at Cernavoda, on the Danube River.

Car plants operated by Renault-owned Dacia and Ford are to temporarily halt production until August 19, voluntarily cutting electricity consumption by around 200 MW. Major wood-based panel manufacturer Kronospan will gradually suspend part of its production, reducing electricity consumption by up to 50 per cent, BIRN has learned.

The measures follow a government meeting with representatives of the largest industrial consumers on Monday at which interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan urged companies to reduce or reschedule electricity consumption, particularly during the evening peak hours.

“We are facing a regional energy crisis. Between 7 p.m. and 11 p.m. we have a significant electricity deficit, which we are covering through imports,” Bolojan said. He also called on households, local authorities and public institutions to voluntarily reduce electricity consumption during the evening peak.

He added that Romania had discussed emergency electricity imports with Ukraine, including possible supplies from one of the country’s nuclear power plants.

The government declared a nationwide alert in the energy sector on July 31 for the entire month of August, citing severe drought and exceptionally low water levels in the Danube and other rivers.

Romania’s sole nuclear power plant at Cernavodă shut down one of its two reactors late last week. The continuing fall in the Danube’s water level is also threatening the plant’s second reactor, raising the prospect of a further drop in domestic electricity production. The Cernavoda plant supplies around one-fifth of Romania’s electricity.

In an emergency operation on Monday, the Romanian Navy detonated a massive rock formation obstructing the flow of water towards a Danube branch supplying the Cernavoda plant. Authorities hope the intervention will allow the remaining reactor to continue operating beyond the four to five days it was expected to remain online if water levels continued falling at the current rate.

Low water levels on the Danube are expected to continue threatening operations at Cernavoda at least until mid-August.

Energy experts say the authorities’ decision to reduce electricity consumption by both industry and households should help stabilise the system in the short term.

However, Romania lacks a coherent national energy strategy, according to energy expert Ciprian Cherciu. “Romania should have invested more in refurbishing its hydropower plants and building new generating capacity, as well as in expanding wind and solar energy, which could provide an alternative when the nuclear plant cannot operate at full capacity, as is the case now”, Cherciu said.

“Above all, Romania should have invested in developing electricity storage capacity. This is an area where the country remains significantly underdeveloped”, he added.

World.title: Hungary Narrowly Avoids Full Nuclear Shutdown; Slovenia Plant Still at Full Capacity
World.content:
Hungary managed to avoid a complete shutdown of its sole nuclear power plant on Tuesday morning as the low water levels in the Danube river caused by the drought began rising, the country’s prime minister, Peter Magyar, announced on X.

“Around 1:30 a.m., we came within a couple of millimeters of a complete shutdown of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, but then the water level stopped dropping, and by morning it had risen by 1.5 centimeters. The last turbine is currently operating safely. Onward to Paks!” Magyar posted.

He added that, “We have just come through the most difficult and critical night so far”, though the situation at the Paks plant has been getting steadily worse since water levels in the Danube began dropping dangerously low last week amid the drought conditions afflicting much of the region. In Budapest, the national water authority measured the Danube’s water level at 23 centimetres on the morning of July 29, well below the previous all-time low of 33 centimetres set in 2018.

The lack of cooling water meant the Paks operator was forced to gradually power down until the plant was operating at about 10 per cent of capacity with one remaining turbine. Hungary relies on Paks for about 42 per cent of its electricity supply.

The problem for Paks is that it uses a direct, once-through (open-cycle) cooling system, which pumps water directly from the Danube to chill its condensers. The system is shared by another nuclear plant situated on the Danube, Romania’s Cernavoda. On Monday, the country’s navy carried out controlled explosions to successfully divert the flow of the river toward the plant, where one of the two reactors is currently shut down.

By contrast, Slovenia’s Krsko Nuclear Power Plant (NEK), built using US Westinghouse technology, continues to operate at full capacity with the cooling tower system operating and respecting the restrictions associated with the Sava River, NEK announced on Monday.

At times of low flows in the Sava and high temperatures, NEK uses a cooling tower system for additional cooling in the third cooling circuit to ensure compliance with environmental restrictions. However, due to the higher electricity consumption to operate the cooling towers and the decrease in the thermodynamic efficiency of the secondary circuit, the efficiency and output of the power plant are reduced and, consequently, the amount of electricity produced is also reduced, NEK explained.

“NEK has informed the competent institutions that we are approaching circumstances in which, due to environmental restrictions related to the Sava River, it will be necessary to reduce the power of the reactor, and in the most unfavourable scenario, to gradually stop the power plant,” NEK said.

Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, said the country’s two nuclear plants, sited on the Vah and Hron rivers, remain unaffected thanks to the similar cooling tower systems used at the Slovenian plant.

World.title: Bulgaria Dismantles Country’s First Fentanyl Lab After Sofia Raid
World.content:
Bulgarian authorities dismantled the country’s first documented fentanyl manufacturing facility on Tuesday and arrested three suspects on location, the General Directorate for Combating Organised Crime said.

The lab was located in the Sofia far-end neighbourhood of Fakulteta. Special police found high-tech equipment capable of producing up to ten kilograms of the lethal narcotic daily.

“The main producers have been detained and charges are about to be filed, with further arrests expected,” Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said on Tuesday. “The laboratory is extremely sophisticated and the operation is being conducted under strict safety measures because of the danger posed by the fumes.”

“The operational work of the officers began in April, when we caught four deals, which indicated that the distribution route led to the Fakulteta neighbourhood – from there the drug is distributed throughout the entire country,” Lyubomir Nikolov, Acting Secretary General of the Ministry of Interior, told National television.

The operation is ongoing.

In June, 11 people were arrested for fentanyl possession in the same neighbourhood. In July, a 42-year-old woman from the same area was arrested for dealing in the drug.

Although the presence of fentanyl in Bulgaria has been talked about by health and addiction prevention activists, authorities have rarely commented on the actual size of the problem.

Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid originally developed for pain management, particularly in surgical and cancer care settings. According to the US National Institute on Drug Abuse, it is roughly 50 to 100 times more potent than morphine.

Illicitly manufactured fentanyl has flooded the illegal drug market in North America and other regions, including Europe. Dealers often mix it into heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine, weed and counterfeit prescription pills. Many users are not aware that fentanyl is present, which can lead to accidental overdoses.

On June 10, a report by the European Union Drug Agency indicated that from 2024 to 2025 there were more than 100 cases of overdoses in Bulgaria caused by fentanyl.

Earlier this year, a BIRN investigation looked into how illicit opioids, sometimes even more potent than fentanyl, are finding their way into the Balkans, while concerns have also been mounting in Central Europe.

World.title: North Macedonia Opposition Blasts ‘Secret Talks’ on Deal With Bulgaria
World.content:
North Macedonia’s Foreign Minister Timco Mucunski. Photo: North Macedonia’s MFA.

North Macedonia’s main opposition party, the Social Democrats, SDSM, accused Foreign Minister Timco Mucunski on Tuesday of holding “secret talks” about the country’s EU future behind the backs of its citizens.

“There is no normal country where a foreign minister says talks on the future of the country are a secret for its citizens,” the SDSM said.

The party accused the centre-right VMRO DPMNE-led government of Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski of refusing to disclose details of important alleged negotiations.

The accusations came a day after Mucunski, in an interview with the state news agency MIA, said for the first time that the government was pursuing confidential efforts to find a “lasting and sustainable solution” to the long-running dispute with Bulgaria that has blocked the opening of EU accession talks.

“We are working on a solution, but not a solution at any cost, and not one that would prove unsustainable and bring us back to the situation we are in today,” Mucunski said, adding that revealing details could jeopardise the negotiations.

According to Mucunski, Skopje will not cross established “red lines” in these talks and is seeking guarantees from EU member states that its accession process will become more predictable once the current impasse is resolved.

Although he declined to identify those involved in the contacts, Mucunski suggested discussions were also taking place with several European partners behind closed doors in an attempt to break the years of deadlock.

North Macedonia’s accession talks have repeatedly stalled despite the country becoming an EU candidate back in 2005. After resolving a long-running dispute over its name with Greece, Skopje expected to move swiftly toward membership negotiations.

Instead, since 2020, Bulgaria blocked the process, arguing that North Macedonia had failed to address issues related to history, language and the rights of people who identify as Bulgarian.

An attempt to overcome the deadlock came in 2022 through the so-called French proposal, under which North Macedonia agreed to amend its constitution to include Bulgarians among its constitutionally recognised peoples.

However, the VMRO DPMNE-led government, which came to power in 2024, has stressed it will not act unless it receives guarantees that Bulgaria won’t block the country again, further down the line.

Mucunski’s remarks about quiet efforts to achieve a breakthrough come after the EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos last month called on North Macedonia again to change its constitution to speed up EU membership, making it clear that EU enlargement is not built on guarantees given in advance.

World.title: Election Race Starts As Bulgaria’s Acting President Seeks Full Mandate
World.content:
Bulgaria’s acting President Iliana Iotova has confirmed she will be running in the upcoming presidential elections scheduled for October.

Iotova, who was previously a low-profile Vice-President to Rumen Radev, assumed office in January after Radev resigned in order to become Bulgaria’s Prime Minister. On July 28 the ruling party, Progressive Bulgaria, and the Bulgarian Socialist Party, where Iotova launched her career, officially endorsed her bid to become the permanent President. Two days later an opinion poll gave her a 50 per cent approval rating from members of the public, enough to give her a landslide win. Other opinion polls have indicated a high, but slightly decreased, support for Radev’s government.

“Iotova has quite a comfortable lead”, Zlatina Zehirova, internal politics editor at Dnevnik.bg, told BIRN. “There are about three months until the elections, in which Iotova's opponents will look for ways to make the most of the power imbalances.” Zehirova said Progressive Bulgaria’s support is both a blessing and a curse, because the shaky politics of Radev’s government might reflect negatively on Iotova's campaign.

World.title: When Propaganda Backfires: Lessons from Orban’s Social Media Defeat in Hungary Election
World.content:
Debunkings went more viral

A notable case was when several young people unfurled a huge Ukrainian flag at the Tisza party’s March 15 national holiday rally. Photos of the protest action were taken and rapidly spread by pro-Fidesz outlets and accounts, portraying the incident as evidence of the opposition party’s pro-Ukrainian alignment.

However, the independent outlet 444.hu quickly reported that the protest action had been coordinated by key staff members of a Fidesz-linked digital campaign agency. It also identified the two minors who had unfurled the flag, one of whom later that day posted an Instagram story showing him with the chairman of the Budapest organisation of Fidelitas, Fidesz’s youth wing.

Repsense examined the content database’s dimensions like viral intensity, which means how fast and how far a narrative spreads – a measure “driven mainly by posting speed (sentences per hour), acceleration, and how big the narrative got in its first six hours relative to its final size”. Regarding the flag issue, the original posts reached 28 points on their “Facebook deep-dive” analysis’ viral intensity scoring, while the exposure scored 44, achieving half of its total reach in under an hour – the fastest spread in their Facebook dataset.

“What the data shows is that Hungarian citizens used the same platforms not as passive consumers of propaganda, but as an active counter-disinformation force. This is a dynamic that echoes the earliest promise of social media as a tool for civic resistance, which brings back memories of the Arab Spring,” says Mykolas Katkus, co-founder and CEO of Repsense. “The information environment had developed an immune response – each new provocation only accelerated its own exposure.”

That the truth behind the flag-unfurling was exposed by an independent media outlet highlights the importance of the free press. “I believe that the report is not fully holistic in the sense that we couldn’t make this government change without independent journalists,” emphasises Kata Horvath, a media researcher at the Department of Media and Communication of Eotvos Lorand University in Budapest.

Horvath believes Hungary’s remaining free press did a tremendous job under very trying conditions, uncovering many corruption cases, the truth behind the flag incident and the paedophile scandal. The latter refers to the 2024 resignation of president Katalin Novak after it emerged that she issued a pardon to the former deputy director of a children’s home who had helped cover up child sexual abuse by his superior.

Bulcsu Hunyadi, head of programs at the Budapest-based Political Capital think-tank, says the active communication by trusted and popular experts also proved important in explaining to the public what was really going on.

Repsense’s data shows similar patterns regarding the divergence between independent pollsters showing the opposition’s advantage and Fidesz-aligned institutes that predicted the governing party would win again. This issue became a narrative thread itself; in the report’s comparison, a poll by the Fidesz-aligned Nezopont Institute scored 15 on the viral intensity index, while the counter-response scored 35.

An AI-generated video featuring a Hungarian father being executed, part of Fidesz’s efforts to frame the vote as a choice between staying out of the war in Ukraine or joining it, scored 28 points, while its counter-narratives got 35. Repsense found that this was one of the most negatively received pieces of campaign-produced content. While these negative reactions could have been towards Ukraine or simply a human reaction, the surrounding discourse, rather than the sentiment score itself, suggests a backlash against the video itself. The most negatively received narrative threads, however, concerned physical attacks on activists.

The pattern was not universal, however: in the widely discussed case of a Ukrainian cash-in-transit seizure that was heavily used for propaganda purposes by the pro-government media, Repsense measured the original narrative and the counter-narrative at the same viral intensity.

World.title: Ticket Out: A Serbian’s Journey from Mercenary in Ukraine to Gangland Hitman
World.content:
For years, Aleksandar Dinic kept a bullet as a souvenir of the war in Ukraine.

Police found it among his belongings in January, when they arrested the 35-year-old Serbian citizen on suspicion of murder.

His alleged victim, a 43-year-old man, was shot dead on January 16 at the foot of Mount Avala, on the outskirts of the Serbian capital, Belgrade.

The dead man is believed to have been part of a Balkan drug cartel and was on trial at the time in Belgrade, accused alongside others of smuggling 324 kilograms of cocaine from South America to Europe.

Organised crime prosecutors in Belgrade suspect that Dinic was hired as a contract killer by the Montenegro-based Kavac criminal clan, according to case files seen by BIRN.

Since 2015, dozens of people have been killed in a gang war between the Kavac and Skaljari clans, which trace their roots to two neighbourhoods of the Montenegrin coastal town of Kotor.

Fighting erupted after 300 kilograms of cocaine vanished from an apartment in the Spanish city of Valencia. Skaljari member Goran Radoman was among the first to die, shot dead in his Belgrade garage.

Since then, the feud has gone global, claiming victims in Montenegro, Serbia, Turkey, Austria, Greece, Spain and other countries.

Dinic had no direct involvement in the gang war, but he did have experience fighting with pro-Russian forces in eastern Ukraine and was on the lookout for some extra cash.

World.title: Croatia to Experience Peak Heat on Thursday With Temperatures Up to 42 Degrees
World.content:
August the 5th, 2026 – Croatia is currently under a particularly strong heat dome, with the peak of that heat set to beat down on the country on Thursday. In some areas, the temperatures could reach a dizzying 42 degrees.

Index reports that a very powerful “heat dome” traps extremely hot air over southern and southeastern parts of the continent. According to meteorologists from Severe Weather Europe, the hottest conditions are expected over the Balkans, Italy, Greece, and parts of the western Mediterranean, with some locations forecast to reach or exceed 42 degrees.

For Croatia, the forecast indicates that temperatures will continue climbing through the week, with Thursday expected to be the peak of the heatwave. Inland parts of the country face the highest temperatures, potentially approaching 42 degrees, while the Adriatic coast will also experience very hot weather, although sea breezes should keep coastal temperatures somewhat lower than inland areas.

a high pressure system from north africa

The extreme heat is being driven by a strong high-pressure system stretching from North Africa into southern and central Europe. This atmospheric pattern allows very warm air from the Sahara to spread northward while preventing cooler Atlantic air from moving into the region. As a result, the hot weather is expected to persist for several days.

Meteorologists warn that the prolonged high temperatures significantly increase health risks, especially for older adults, young children, and people with chronic medical conditions. Authorities advise people to stay hydrated, avoid all kinds of more strenuous outdoor activities during the hottest part of the day, seek shade or air-conditioned spaces whenever and wherever possible, and check on vulnerable family members and neighbours.

The article also highlights an increased wildfire risk all across southern Europe. The combination of extreme heat, dry vegetation, and periods of gusty winds creates conditions where fires can ignite easily and spread rapidly. Fire services across several Mediterranean countries remain on heightened alert.

a colder front is coming!

Looking beyond the peak heat, the forecast suggests that a cold front will begin moving into central Europe later in the week, bringing thunderstorms to some regions and a noticeable drop in temperatures. Croatia is expected to see this change after Thursday, although forecasters caution that any storms accompanying the front could be locally severe, with heavy rain, strong wind gusts, hail, and frequent lightning possible.

Overall, the article’s main message is that Thursday is expected to be the most dangerous day of the current heatwave in Croatia, with temperatures possibly reaching 42 degrees in some inland areas before a cooler, more unstable weather pattern arrives later in the week.

World.title: Bizarre Medieval “Vampire” Found in Pakrac Cemetery
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – An extremely bizarre Medieval “vampire” has been found in a Pakrac cemetery, with archaeologists believing that the particular method of burial was to “prevent the vampire returning among the living”.

Index reports that a very mysterious medieval burial discovered at the Stari Grad Pakrac archaeological site has once again brought attention to ancient beliefs about vampires and the fear of the dead returning among the living. Archaeologists uncovered the remains of a person buried face down, an unusual burial position that experts believe may have been an intentional ritual. According to archaeologist Krešimir Vacek, the way the body was placed suggests that people of the time wanted to prevent the deceased from returning after death.

The “vampire” burial likely dates back to the late 13th century and was found at a medieval cemetery connected with the former settlement around Stari Grad Pakrac. Archaeologists have been researching the site for years, uncovering numerous graves and important historical remains.

This is not the first unusual discovery of its kind at the location. Earlier excavations revealed another so-called “vampire” burial, a skeleton inside a valuable sarcophagus that was missing its human head. Instead, researchers found animal remains believed to be part of a horse skull. Such practices were linked to medieval beliefs that certain people could return from the grave and harm the living.

In medieval Europe, fears of supernatural forces were widespread, and communities sometimes carried out unusual burial practices when they believed someone could become a threat after death. The latest discovery in Pakrac offers another rare insight into the beliefs, fears, and rituals of people who lived more than 800 years ago.

World.title: Animal Rights Group Sparks Debate After Tragic Zagreb Zoo Lioness Death
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – A prominent Croatian animal rights group Friends of Animals (Prijatelji životinja) has sparked fresh debate after the tragic death of a lioness at the jaws of a male line at Zagreb Zoo.

Index reports that an ongoing debate over the role and funding of zoological gardens has returned to the public scene in Croatia. It comes after the aforementioned animal rights organisation strongly criticised the way public money is used to support zoos, arguing that people contribute financially even if they never visit them.

The organisation claims that many people are unaware that municipal budgets are used to finance the operation of zoological gardens. According to Prijatelji životinja, taxpayers are effectively contributing to institutions they may never personally use, raising questions about whether public funds should support facilities that keep animals in captivity.

Their criticism focuses on the belief that the traditional zoo model is outdated and that keeping wild animals in enclosed spaces cannot fully meet their natural needs. The group argues that resources should instead be directed towards alternative approaches to animal protection and conservation.

A long-running debate over the purpose of modern zoos

The controversy reflects a much wider global discussion about the role of zoological gardens in the 21st century. Supporters of modern zoos argue that they are no longer simply places where visitors come to see exotic animals. Many contemporary institutions focus on education, scientific research, species protection and breeding programmes aimed at helping endangered animals.

Critics, however, question whether these goals justify keeping animals in captivity. Prijatelji životinja argues that no enclosure can truly replace an animal’s natural habitat and that conservation efforts should focus more heavily on protecting species in the wild.

Public funding remains at the very heart of the discussion

The financial side of the debate has become one of the main points of disagreement.

Prijatelji životinja has previously highlighted examples of cities allocating significant amounts of public money to maintain zoos, arguing that citizens who do not support the concept are still indirectly financing it through taxes. Supporters of zoological gardens, however, point out that these institutions provide educational programmes, contribute to biodiversity awareness and participate in international conservation projects. Modern zoos increasingly present themselves as centres for protecting endangered species rather than simply tourist attractions.

Zagreb Zoo highlights conservation and education

The debate comes at a time when the role of zoos continues to evolve. The Zoological Garden of the City of Zagreb promotes programmes focused on animal care, public education and conservation activities. The institution also offers initiatives such as animal adoption programmes, through which citizens can financially support the care of individual animals while they remain residents of the zoo. The zoo has also highlighted its involvement in international projects aimed at protecting wildlife and raising awareness about biodiversity.

A question with no easy answers…

The disagreement between animal protection organisations and zoo supporters is unlikely to disappear. For critics, the issue is about whether society should continue funding a model based on keeping wild animals in captivity. For supporters, zoos remain important centres for education, research and conservation.

As public discussions about animal welfare become increasingly prominent, the future of zoological gardens will likely depend on how successfully they can balance their traditional role with modern expectations about conservation, ethics and animal wellbeing.

World.title: Croatian High-Tech Trains: The Innovation Transforming Rail Transport
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – Croatian high-tech trains are the domestic innovation transforming rail transport as the country enters a new era of railway transport.

As Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni, that era is being strongly driven by one of the country’s most advanced industrial achievements – modern trains developed and produced by Končar.

Often described as among the most complex technological products created by Croatian industry, these new-generation trains represent a combination of domestic engineering, advanced technology and a push towards greener transport solutions. Over 70 percent of their components are Croatian-made, while key systems and subsystems, including control systems, communication technology, traction transformers and other essential elements, are produced within the Končar Group.

To date, Končar has delivered 70 new-generation low-floor trains to Croatian railways, including 40 units delivered in less than five years. The company has also recently signed new agreements with HŽ Passenger Transport for six battery-electric trains and the construction of a hybrid charging station in Kotoriba, with a total value of 53.6 million euros.

Croatia’s first battery trains enter service

One of the biggest milestones has been the development of Končar’s battery-powered trains, which represent a major technological step for Croatia and one of the first examples of this type of commercial railway technology in Europe.

The battery-electric multiple unit (BEMV) uses fully electric propulsion, powered by onboard batteries as well as existing overhead electrical networks. This makes it particularly suitable for Croatia, where a significant part of the railway network is still not electrified. This type of technology allows the trains to operate on both electrified and non-electrified routes, creating a more sustainable solution for passenger transport across the country.

The train was designed for daily operation of up to 480 kilometres and up to 18 hours of service per day. On non-electrified lines, it can reach speeds of up to 120 km/h using battery power, while on electrified routes it can achieve speeds of up to 160 km/h. Another highly important innovation is the battery motor train (BMV), designed specifically for routes without overhead electrical infrastructure. It can reach speeds of up to 120 km/h and, depending on conditions, can travel more than 200 kilometres during testing on a single charge.

Designed for modern passengers

The new trains are not only focused on efficiency and sustainability but also on improving passenger comfort. They include wheelchair access ramps, dedicated bicycle spaces, accessible toilets, video surveillance, passenger information screens, audio announcements and free Wi-Fi. The trains can also be connected with other new-generation low-floor units already operating in Croatia, allowing increased capacity when needed.

A major investment in greener mobility

The development of these trains is part of the project “Application of Green Technologies in Railway Passenger Transport”, financed through Croatia’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan. Several charging stations have already been opened at railway stations in cities including Split, Osijek, Varaždin, Bjelovar, Virovitica and Pula. Further expansion is planned, with additional battery and hybrid trains expected to enter service in the coming years. A wider project financed through a European Investment Bank loan, worth almost €118 million, includes the delivery of additional trains and charging infrastructure.

New trains to connect Zagreb and Split

Končar is also preparing a new generation of long-distance trains that will connect Zagreb and Split.

The route between the two cities stretches for 429 kilometres, but only around a quarter of the line is electrified. Because of this, the new trains will combine electric and diesel propulsion, allowing them to operate efficiently across different sections of the route. The trains will reach speeds of up to 160 km/h and will be capable of connecting multiple units together to increase capacity. The first six trains are part of a larger agreement between Končar and HŽ Passenger Transport covering 19 new low-floor trains. Additional units are planned to connect cities including Osijek, Rijeka and Pula.

Croatian engineering on the international stage

The latest generation of Končar trains highlights the growing role of Croatian industry in advanced manufacturing and sustainable technology.

From battery-powered rail vehicles to modern mobility solutions, these projects show that Croatian companies are capable of developing complex products that compete in a highly demanding global market. As railway transport across Europe moves towards lower emissions and smarter infrastructure, Croatia’s domestically produced trains are becoming a symbol of innovation, engineering expertise and the country’s ambitions beyond traditional industries.

World.title: Croatian Pizza Prices Spark Debate as Bill Goes Viral
World.content:
August the 4th, 2026 – Croatian pizza prices have sparked fresh debate as a bill of 32 euros issued in Stari Grad on Hvar goes viral across social media.

Debates over prices on the Croatian coast have once again erupted on social media, with a restaurant bill from the island of Hvar becoming the latest trigger for a wider discussion about the cost of summer holidays in Croatia. Poslovni reports that this latest price-related controversy began after a guest shared a receipt from a pizzeria in Stari Grad, where a large pizza cost 22 euros. The post quickly spread online, dividing opinions between two opposing camps.

Some users described such prices as completely unreasonable and a sign of growing greed in the tourism sector. Others argued that restaurants clearly display their menus and prices, meaning guests can see the costs in advance and decide whether they want to order. The fact that another seaside bill became a viral topic highlights how strongly food and service prices continue to shape conversations during every tourist season. The debate has grown beyond the price of one pizza, becoming part of a larger discussion about Croatia’s tourism model.

22 euros is steep compared to a 7.50 euro pizza in italy

Soon, visitors began sharing their own experiences and comparing Croatian coastal prices with those in other popular European destinations. One social media user compared the situation with southern Italy, saying that in a restaurant in Ercolano, near Naples, a pizza cost just 7.50 euros, a beer 3 euros, and a bottle of white wine 10 euros.

Others shared less positive experiences from Croatian islands. One visitor said that while the island of Vis was beautiful, the prices were too high. She described paying €120 per person for a seven-hour speedboat excursion that included visits to three caves and two beaches, but without lunch included. She also pointed out that entering one of the caves cost an additional €15, even for those who chose to swim there themselves.

However, not everyone believes the criticism is justified. Some commenters argued that visitors simply choose where they travel and where they eat according to their own budgets. “Everyone goes where the food and prices suit them,” one comment said, summarising the opinion of those who believe customers have the final choice.

Many also pointed out that high prices will continue as long as there is demand and people willing to pay them.

“While there are people who will gladly pay 22 euros for a pizza, there will be prices like this. But tourism cannot rely on this forever,” one user wrote, warning that the current model may not be sustainable in the long term. Others noted that expensive pizzas are not only found on the coast, mentioning examples from Zagreb as well, expanding the discussion beyond seasonal tourism.

An even more expensive pizza becomes the symbol of the debate

The most attention, however, was attracted by a comment from a man who claimed that he had seen an even more expensive pizza on the island of Brač. “There are also pizzas for 32 euros. If it doesn’t suit you, the door is open for you to leave and go elsewhere,” he wrote.

The comment quickly became a symbol of the argument that prices are ultimately determined by supply and demand, with businesses charging what customers are prepared to pay. Another theory that appeared in the discussion was that some tourists deliberately visit the most expensive restaurants so they can later complain online and share their bills on social media, gaining attention. “They go there on purpose so they can complain about high prices afterwards,” one commenter suggested.

Guests complain, but the spending continues…

Although complaints about Croatian prices return every summer, financial data paints a more complex picture. Examples of expensive bills continue to circulate online, including a case of visitors from neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina who reportedly paid more than 50 euros for a jumbo pizza and two coffees near Dubrovnik, as well as a British tourist who paid a whole 42 euros for just two drinks in Split.

However, spending figures show that tourists are still opening their wallets. According to data from Croatia’s Tax Administration, consumer spending during the summer months has continued to grow. In July, the total value of fiscalised receipts increased by almost 24 percent compared with the same month last year, reaching 6.8 billion euros.

The hospitality sector also recorded growth, with more than seven percent more receipts issued and their total value increasing by over 11 percent. Tourism analysts say this shows that visitors continue to spend despite complaints, although they warn that such a trend may not be sustainable forever.

The picture is not the same everywhere

A closer look at the tourism sector shows that success is not evenly distributed. While luxury hotels and high-end campsites are recording strong occupancy and increased revenue, many small private accommodation providers and some restaurants are facing difficulties. June 2026’s figures showed a decline of seven percent in arrivals and six percent in overnight stays compared with the previous year, with the largest drops recorded in Istria, Kvarner and Zadar County.

The data suggests a growing divide within Croatian tourism. Luxury segments continue to perform well, while businesses offering average services at increasingly high prices are finding it harder to attract guests. Tourists appear to be paying closer attention to value for money and are becoming less willing to spend large amounts on experiences that do not match the expected quality.

Market rules apply, but guests are becoming more demanding

Tourism experts have repeatedly warned about price increases that are not matched by improvements in quality. While the government and the Ministry of Tourism have called for more reasonable pricing policies, Boris Žgomba, president of the Croatian Chamber of Commerce’s Association of Travel Agencies, has stressed that prices are ultimately determined by the market and the relationship between supply and demand. Croatia has positioned itself alongside other Mediterranean destinations such as Italy and Spain in terms of pricing, while Dubrovnik regularly ranks among the most expensive cities in the region.

At the same time, travellers are increasingly searching for authentic experiences, local culture and quieter destinations. This could create opportunities for parts of Croatia’s tourism industry that adapt to changing expectations.

If prices continue rising without a corresponding improvement in quality, some tourists may turn towards more affordable destinations such as Albania, which has experienced strong tourism growth by attracting visitors who find Croatia or Greece too expensive. As another busy summer season unfolds, prices on the Croatian coast and islands remain one of the most debated topics in Croatia, raising a continuing question: where is the line between market logic and genuine hospitality?

World.title: Is Spending in July in Croatia Really Breaking Records?
World.content:
August the 3rd, 2026 – Tax Authority data for spending in July in Croatia shows continued growth in fiscalised spending, but the nominal figures need to be interpreted with caution.

Higher receipt totals don’t actually necessarily mean that residents and tourists bought more goods and services, because part of the increase comes from higher prices. Index writes that in order to assess the real trend in consumption it is necessary to remove the effect of inflation. When nominal data are adjusted for price rises, the real growth is noticeably weaker, and in some periods and sectors spending stagnates or even falls.

price increases are largely responsible for nominal growth

According to Tax Authority data on fiscalised spending, food-and-beverage preparation and serving activities as well as the accommodation sector in Croatia recorded strong growth during the summer months, with a clear seasonal jump towards July. The cumulative change compared with the previous period is positive, and growth is also visible in the monthly figures.

In food-and-beverage preparation and serving, fiscalised turnover during the month of July reached 891 million euros nominally, or 860 million euros when adjusted for inflation. In the same month last year the turnover stood at 802 million euros. This means the nominal value of receipts increased by around 11 percent, while real growth after removing the effect of higher prices was about 7 percent.

Cumulatively, from the beginning of the year to the end of July, turnover in hospitality was 11 percent higher nominally than in the same period last year. After correction for inflation the real growth stood at 6.5 percent. In other words, guests and residents did spend more than last year, but the difference is not as large as the nominal figures suggest because part of the rise stems from higher prices of food and drink.

a look at accommodation

Results by county are highly uneven. While some counties recorded real growth in fiscalised accommodation turnover of more than 30 percent, others saw double-digit declines. Most Adriatic counties achieved moderate growth, yet even on the coast the results are not uniform. In some counties turnover rose by only a few percent, while Dubrovnik-Neretva County recorded a slight real decline of 0.6 percent.

Extreme results in individual counties should be interpreted cautiously; they may be the consequence of a low comparative base, changes in coverage or local specifics rather than a dramatic shift in overall tourist activity. During July, fiscalised turnover in the accommodation sector reached 691 million euros nominally, compared with 630 million euros in the same month last year – a nominal increase of 9.7 percent. After removing the impact of inflation this year’s turnover amounts to 667 million euros, meaning it was 5.9 percent higher in real terms than in July last year. Guests therefore left almost ten percent more money for accommodation, but the actual growth in consumption was closer to six percent.

was july 2026 really more successful than july 2025?

The data show that fiscalised turnover in July was higher than last year in both hospitality and accommodation, even after adjustment for inflation. Nevertheless, real growth was significantly weaker than the nominal figures, and results vary considerably between sectors and counties.

It can therefore be concluded that July was better than last year’s according to the indicators examined, but not that the season was dramatically or unequivocally more successful. Tax Authority data are currently the most reliable publicly available indicator of fiscalised spending, yet they do not cover every element of the tourist result. An important methodological change should also be noted: from this year the Tax Authority’s reporting includes payments via transaction accounts. In order to keep the data comparable with the previous year, those payments have been excluded from this analysis.

The conclusion is therefore cautious: nominal spending is rising, but once inflation is taken into account the picture is considerably more moderate. The figures show seasonal growth and large regional differences, but they do not unambiguously confirm that this year’s July was significantly more successful.

World.title: Meet Taljurić, The Strange Croatian Fingerprint Island
World.content:
August the 3rd, 2026 – Taljurić, (or Pijat if you’re local) is a strange formation, it’s a totally flat Croatian island that resembles a human fingerprint and has absolutely zero vegetation on it.

The Adriatic might look calm and alluring during summer, but it’s no stranger to surprisingly violent storms and winds. When they hit, the usually calm Adriatic becomes very choppy and washes over almost its entire surface repeatedly. Putni kofer writes that over countless centuries, these repeated actions have made it appear like a flat stone plate laid carefully in the middle of the open, unforgiving sea.

Wherever you look along Croatia’s heavily indented, rugged and island-laden coastline, something takes your breath away. Be it stunning beaches, pebbles and rocks of every shape, secret coves, water shifting from transparent turquoise to deep blue, shores battered by waves on one side and watched over by powerful mountains on the other… The list goes on. Then there are the 1,000+ islands, small and large, bare and green, low and steep, and some of the most unusual shapes imaginable. Some have been inhabited for thousands of years; others hold only a lighthouse, a lonely chapel or traces of former farming. A few are so tiny and exposed that almost nothing can grow on them. Among these rocky outcrops lie some of the strangest sights on the Croatian coast.

From Galešnjak and Baljenac to… Pijat, (Taljurić)

Some of these islands have gained worldwide recognition. Galešnjak, thanks to its almost perfect heart shape, became known as the Island of Love. Baljenac (also called Bavljenac), seen from the air, resembles a giant human fingerprint – an effect created by the dense, tangled network of dry-stone walls that once enclosed tiny agricultural plots. In this sea of bizarre shapes lies another islet whose appearance is perfectly captured by its name. It is called Taljurić (locally also known as Pijat). Viewed from the sea or from the air, it really does look like a large stone plate carefully placed on the surface of the Adriatic.

Taljurić lies within the boundaries of the remarkable Telašćica Nature Park, on the south-eastern part of Dugi otok, and is regarded as one of the most unusual natural phenomena of this protected area. Official documents list it as a rock (hrid) and rank it among the smallest islands and rocks in the park’s archipelago. It measures about 60 metres in diameter and rises only three metres above the sea.

In essence, it is an almost flat stone slab made of horizontally layered limestone. Its upper surface has been continuously exposed to waves, salt and wind, so the whole islet looks as if the sea has been grinding and levelling it for centuries. During powerful storms the waves can sweep across nearly its entire surface – which explains why no vegetation has ever managed to take hold.

no vegetation manages to take hold on taljurić

Its unusual appearance directly influenced its name. The islet resembles a flat, round board of the kind once used in kitchens, which Venetian sailors called “tagliero” in their dialect. According to Telašćica Nature Park, the name Taljurić, which isn’t frequently used by locals, developed from that word. There are absolutely no trees, bushes or grass on the surface. Although from a distance it looks completely barren, its edge is not lifeless. On the rocks just above the waterline live colonies of barnacles (known locally as brambuljci), tiny marine crustaceans that cling tightly to the stone and withstand the constant pounding of the waves.

Another curiosity lies on the south-western side of Pijat: the remains of a former fossil cave whose roof eroded away over geological time. Today it looks like a cave open to the sky – a stone hollow without a ceiling. The sea around the islet is rich in life, and the wider Telašćica area includes valuable marine habitats such as posidonia meadows, underwater cliffs, reefs and sea caves.
