To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

612th day of protests in Tbilisi

World.title: Breaking: Firefighters union boss exerted 'extraordinary' influence, report finds
World.content:
Victoria's anti-corruption watchdog has found serious and concerning conduct by senior public officers, including ministers, MPs and public servants, during a bitter pay dispute with the state's firefighters union.

But the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC) has stopped short of making any findings of corrupt conduct, instead warning such behaviour raised the risk of corruption.

IBAC found that senior members of government acted contrary to established policies, procedures, codes of conduct and conventions in negotiating a deal with United Firefighters Union (UFU) secretary Peter Marshall without the knowledge and involvement of the responsible minister, agencies and departments.

"By doing so, the government placed itself in a position where Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence over the negotiations," the report read.

Mr Marshall was also given privileged access to senior government figures.

Peter Marshall is the secretary of the United Firefighters Union in Victoria. (ABC News: Leanne Wong)

The IBAC investigation examined allegations of corruption during the bitter industrial dispute between firefighters union, the Country Fire Authority, and the government of former premier Daniel Andrews.

The investigation began in 2018 and looked into the matter as far back as Mr Andrews's first term in office.

In 2014, the militant United Firefighters Union ran a concerted campaign against the then-Coalition government over pay and conditions.

Daniel Andrews was Victorian premier at the time of the enterprise bargaining negotiations. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Mr Andrews promised to respect firefighters, increase their numbers and overhaul the way firefighting operated in Victoria.

But upon coming to office after the 2014 election, Mr Andrews gave the job of emergency services minister to Jane Garrett, who resisted the union's demands.

The issue came to a head in 2016, with Mr Andrews intervening to end the impasse.

The move forced Ms Garrett, who died from cancer in 2022, to resign, and fuelled allegations the union had been given a sweetheart deal.

IBAC's probe is understood to have included interviews with Mr Andrews and senior ministers, however witnesses are unable to confirm or deny if they have been spoken to under IBAC's laws.

World.title: Blistering Marsh knock helps Sunrisers smash Hundred's record score
World.content:
A brutal assault by Mitch Marsh has proved the launch pad for a record total by Leeds Sunrisers in The Hundred competition at Headingley.

The West Australian battered 76 off 37 balls with seven sixes to send the franchise on its way to 2-241 off 100 balls, the highest score in the competition's six years, 15 runs better than the previous record.

Opponents London Spirit were never in the hunt on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST), despite finishing with 6-204 themselves.

Marsh and Ryan Rickelton broke the record for the highest partnership for any wicket in the competition, 148 from 65 balls.

"I'm very routine on game day, trying to stay relaxed, which I am not, but once I get started I try and get into the game and build partnerships," said Marsh.

"Partnerships are very important to us."

The 34-year-old, who now has 290 runs in five innings for Sunrisers with a lowest score of 41, added he loves batting at Headingley, where he also made a run-a-ball Ashes century in 2023.

The carnage continued after Marsh's dismissal with South African Rickelton slamming an unbeaten 94 off 42 balls and local hero Harry Brook carving 55 off 18 deliveries with some astonishing shots.

Adam Zampa (pictured) copped the brunt of the punishment from his Australian teammate Marsh. (Getty Images: Phillip Brown)

Among the mauled bowlers was Aussie leg-spinner Adam Zampa, whose 10 deliveries went for 33 with one dot ball and four sixes.

His first set of five balls, to Marsh, went for 25: six, four, six, wide, six, dot, with the last ball following a strategic time-out mid-set.

Zampa's second set came immediately after Marsh's dismissal, caught at deep cover miscuing a drive.

Andrew Tye's 20 balls went for a relatively creditable 42.

"Hell of a lot of fun," said Brook.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I thought the way Mitch Marsh and Ryan Rickelton started was incredible. Not seen anyone hit the ball as hard as Marsh.

"Marsh loves batting here. Rickelton got more runs, but he really set the tone in those first 50 balls," said former England bowler Stuart Broad on commentary.

London Spirit never got going in response, losing Yorkshire favourite Jonny Bairstow for a second-ball duck and slumping to 5-56.

Nathan Ellis dismissed the danger man, Liam Livingstone, for an 11-ball 34, and took 2-42 in his 20.

After Donald Brevis went for 38 off 21 balls, David Willey, with 83 not out off 46 balls, helped Spirit rescue their net run-rate, but the destination of the night's points had long been decided.

AAP

World.title: Erectile dysfunction drug may heighten risk of eye disease, study shows
World.content:
Men who use a Viagra-like erectile dysfunction drug long-term are "significantly more likely" to develop glaucoma than those who do not, according to a new study.

The research, published in the British Journal of Ophthalmology, followed 74,000 men aged 40 years and older, half of whom had been prescribed tadalafil (sold under the brand names such as Cialis) over a period of five years.

Along with its use to treat erectile dysfunction, the drug is also used for the long-term treatment of urinary tract problems such as increased urgency associated with an enlarged prostate.

The researchers found people who used the drug long-term were 22 per cent more likely to develop glaucoma — a common eye disease which often leads to blindness — than those who did not.

"This is the first cohort study to show there is a correlation between taking these medications and an increased risk of developing glaucoma," said Flora Hui, an optometrist and research fellow at the Centre for Eye Research Australia, who did not contribute to the study.

Dr Hui said while the study showed the risk of having glaucoma was "statistically higher" in those who took the drug, the overall risk was still "quite low".

But, she said, it highlighted the importance of getting eyes tested before, and during the time of taking these medications, especially if a person had glaucoma risk factors.

"If you're a bit older, especially if you have a family history of glaucoma … and if you're going to be on long-term therapy, you really need to have regular eye tests because glaucoma can be largely symptomless."

Glaucoma can lead to permanent vision loss. (Getty Images: Tetra Images)

PDE5i drugs and eye health

Tadalafil is part of a class of drugs called phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (PDE5i), a group which also includes sildenafil (sold under the brand name Viagra).

Previous studies have linked PDE5i drugs with ophthalmological side effects, including those that affect the optic nerve, but until now, there has not been any research showing a strong link between a person taking tadalafil long-term and then developing glaucoma.

'Silent thief of sight' A headache is a common occurrence for many of us, but for Effie, it was the first sign that she had glaucoma.

PDE5i inhibitors block a protein called PDE-5, increasing blood flow to the penis and helping people develop and maintain an erection.

They also relax muscle tissue and improve blood flow in organs such as the prostate and bladder.

While scientists still do not know exactly how these drugs increased a person's risk of developing glaucoma, Dr Hui said there were a few working theories.

People had a finite amount of blood in their body, Dr Hui said, which meant it had to "pull the blood from somewhere" to encourage it to go elsewhere.

"We think that maybe it can transiently increase the eye pressure in people on these medications, or maybe it's taking blood away from the optic nerve at the back of the eye, which is what gets affected in glaucoma," Dr Hui said.

"If you're getting transient episodes where you don't get sufficient blood to the nerve, then that can increase the chance of injury to the nerve and then potentially increase your risk of developing glaucoma."

Flora Hui says the study highlighted the need for increased eye health checks. (Supplied: Centre for Eye Research Australia)

Although the study was observational and did not prove that taking tadalafil caused participants to develop glaucoma, Dr Hui said it showed a "clear correlation" between the two, and highlighted the need for more in-depth research.

Andrew White, a clinician scientist ophthalmologist at Westmead Hospital and Westmead Institute for Medical Research, who did not contribute to the study, added that not everyone who took these drugs experienced the same side effects, or had any side effects at all.

Dr White said while some people experienced a temporary increase in pressure in the eye, others experienced low blood pressure.

"One of the other things that we have known for quite a long time is that if your blood pressure is too low or your blood pressure control varies a lot, then your glaucoma can also get worse," he said.

And the more "pressure spikes" someone experienced, the more likely they were to either develop glaucoma or make it worse, Dr White said.

Study participants not 'healthy'

The study, led by researchers from Taiwan, used data from 73,854 men from an international health database called TriNetX, excluding anyone with a history of glaucoma.

Researchers matched 36,927 people who used tadalafil with 36,927 men who did not use any PDE5i drugs.

While the drug is used to treat erectile dysfunction, small doses can also be taken daily over the long term to treat urinary tract symptoms.

The study found those who were prescribed the drug for urinary tract symptoms were 22 per cent more likely to develop glaucoma; 32 per cent more likely to have ocular hypertension and 33 per cent more likely to start glaucoma treatment than those who did not take it.

"Tadalafil use for lower urinary tract symptoms was associated with a significant increase in the risk of glaucoma, ocular hypertension, primary open-angle glaucoma and initiation of glaucoma treatment in a large, multinational, real-world cohort," researchers concluded.

The study found the risk increased in men aged over 50.

Tadalafil is a type of drug known as a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor. (Getty Images: Bloomberg)

The study itself had a number of key limitations, including that most of the participants were white, and therefore the findings may not apply to men of other ethnicities.

And they were not able to factor in changes in medication or the development of other underlying conditions, which could increase someone's risk of developing glaucoma.

And this was important, Dr Hui said, as other variables could affect someone's eye health.

"We're not looking at what we call healthy participants to start with," she said.

"About 40 per cent of them have high blood pressure, about 40 per cent of them have high cholesterol. These people do have comorbidities.

"It's a bit inconclusive about whether the additional chronic conditions made a difference."

Eye health monitoring needed

Although the study found a link between long-term use of tadalafil and glaucoma, the researchers stressed men should not stop using the drug for treatment of urinary tract symptoms.

Instead, they said, it indicated the need to have regular eye checks.

Dr Hui agreed.

"It's sometimes not the first thing we think about when we're taking these medications, but it's really important to get tested before you're starting these medications and if you are currently on them to get regular eye checks as well," she said.

Professor White said good monitoring and early intervention could improve someone's outcomes.

ABC Health in your Instagram feed Follow @abchealth on Instagram, where we're busting myths and sharing practical, smart health advice.

"If there is a reason for you to be monitored more closely, your local optometrist is a great start," he said.

"And the sooner we can pick something up, the sooner we can get on with treatment."

Dr Hui added that, for many, taking erectile dysfunction drugs could greatly improve someone's quality of life.

So a discussion about the potential risks and benefits was something for each patient to weigh up with their doctor.

World.title: Outback town says grid connection key to capturing AI investment
World.content:
As Australia races to build the infrastructure behind the AI boom, an outback Queensland mayor says the next generation of data centres should be built hundreds of kilometres from the nearest city.

Behind the rapid rise of artificial intelligence is a growing network of data centres built to keep up with the spike in demand for computing power and storage.

With about 250 data centres operating across the country, some communities have begun pushing back over their proximity to urban areas.

In the north-west Queensland town of Cloncurry, about 120 kilometres east of Mount Isa, Mayor Greg Campbell says the bush could prove the perfect home for the critical infrastructure.

"I've been talking about data centres with different companies for many years … but in the last month, I've had two return calls from companies," Cr Campbell said.

"I think these companies are trying to get ahead and looking to areas … outside that urban area."

Greg Campbell hopes a concrete timeline for CopperString can give industry certainty in the region. (Supplied: Cloncurry Shire Council)

Data centres hinge on CopperString

Data centres have traditionally required considerable water to transfer heat away from their servers and large energy loads to fuel computing power.

Efficiency gains through closed-loop systems and water recycling in new generations of data centres have reduced the amount of water required, but power remains the biggest hurdle in places like north-west Queensland.

Cloncurry, like all communities across the region, is not connected to the national energy market, relying on decentralised renewable projects and large diesel generators to power the area.

Greg Campbell says the region could be the perfect home for data centres trying to avoid pushback from urban centres. (ABC News: Meghan Dansie)

The state government has committed to connecting the region to the east coast through the CopperString project, but Cr Campbell said there was still no firm timeline for construction.

"CopperString is probably the precursor to turn that interest into a genuine business," he said.

"Because the north west isn't connected to the national electricity market, the mines, predominantly as the biggest users, will say that it's some of the dearest power probably in the world.

" We need that commitment to turn into a deliverable so that these companies can make bankable decisions. "

As demand and reliance on AI grows, perceptions around data centres have shifted. What was once seen as a commercial asset is now viewed as something of strategic importance.

The remote town of Cloncurry is about 120 kilometres east of Mount Isa. (ABC North West Qld: Meghan Dansie)

Australian Strategic Policy Institute deputy director Raelene Lockhorst believes the centres should be viewed as essential infrastructure.

"Where we build data centres is now a national security decision, not just a commercial one," Ms Lockhorst said.

"Northern Australia offers the combination that makes it the natural place to start: abundant land, renewable-energy potential, international cable connectivity, proximity to Indo-Pacific markets and rising strategic importance.

"Rather than retrofitting this infrastructure into already constrained metropolitan areas, the north lets us build Australia's next generation of digital infrastructure where it strengthens both economic development and national resilience."

Raelene Lockhorst says northern Australia's ample space and resources make it the ideal location to expand data centres. (ABC News: Michael Barnett)

Queensland Treasurer David Janetzki said proposed data centres in north-west Queensland could seek support for local energy solutions through the government's $200 million North West Energy Fund.

But the treasurer would not provide a delivery date for the western section of CopperString, saying the government's immediate focus was the eastern link between Townsville and Hughenden.

'Trillion-dollar question'

The United States Studies Centre said Australia's data centre sector had expanded considerably since 2020 and global demand for infrastructure was forecast to double by 2030.

University of Queensland economist Flavio Menezes said guessing how long the investment boom would last was the "trillion-dollar question".

"In 2023, $500 billion of the United States GDP … was data centres and the number keeps going up," Professor Menezes said.

"Data centres are like the heavy industry of this century.

"They produce the computing power that has become really the essential input for our digital economies.

"It [investment] all relies on computing power, and that demand keeps going up … there will be a natural limit for that investment but, if you think about the next two, three, four years, it will keep going up."

Flavio Menezes says understanding how long the data centre boom will last is the "trillion-dollar question". (ABC Radio Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

CopperString's western leg is managed by Queensland Investment Corporation and will rely on private capital to be completed.

Professor Menezes said demand from data centres would help strengthen the business case for CopperString, but warned people to be wary of the drawback.

Flavio Menezes says data centres should be seen as the "heavy industry" of the 21st century. (ABC News: Jerry Rickard)

"Data centres can bring a large number of benefits to the regional economy … the additional demand may make the case for CopperString make more economic sense as well," he said.

"Done well, they can support the case for that connection … but it's important to remember benefits go to the wider community.

"But there's hyperlocal costs in terms of pollution and competition for electricity.

"I wouldn't want to live by one."

World.title: Man dies after car crashes into parked truck in Brisbane's south
World.content:
A man has died after the car he was driving crashed into a parked truck in Brisbane's south in the early hours of this morning.

Emergency services were called to the corner of Freeman Road and Firth Street in Richlands just after 4am.

The male driver of the vehicle was critically injured in the crash and died at the scene.

Anyone who witnessed the crash or has any dash cam footage or CCTV has been asked to come forward.

The Forensic Crash unit is investigating.

The latest government data shows 185 people have been killed on Queensland roads between January 1 and August 2 this year; a 10.1 per cent increase compared to the same time last year.

World.title: Low-allergenic camel meat helps curb feral population
World.content:
It is no easy feat for Tim Carmody to manage and maintain the feral camel population on his 400,000-hectare property on the edge of Western Australia's Gibson Desert.

Feral camels are a persistent pest on pastoral country in central Australia, destroying cattle water points and other infrastructure, and trampling precious vegetation.

Camels can be a major problem for pastoralists, with control costs in the tens of thousands. (ABC Goldfields-Esperance: Andy Tyndall)

The animal is a nationally declared pest and the Western Australian Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development estimates there to be more than 1 million roaming central Australia.

Prenti Downs pastoralist Mr Carmody said it could cost him between $20,000 and $30,000 a year to manage the fluctuating camel numbers.

Tim Carmody is trialling commercial harvesting to control camel populations on his property. (ABC Rural: Tara De Landgrafft)

"They can eat 80 per cent of the vegetation out here, so they're direct competitors to cattle," he said.

"One camel unit is equal to two cow units, so if you've got 500 camel coming through, that's equal to 1,000 head of cattle wandering through your place and at times we can have several thousand."

Camels try to push through steel gates protecting cattle water points on Prenti Downs. (Supplied: Tim Carmody)

Getting value out of feral camels

Mr Carmody engaged a pet food business to kill the camels and use them for meat.

As part of the field operation, Mr Carmody flies his plane to spot camels and guide the shooters in the vehicles on the ground.

"We can take out a mob of 50 or 60 camel in sub an hour," he said.

"We just recover costs. We've been working at and hoping over the years that this will become more of a commercial operation for everyone involved and once it becomes a commercial operation it becomes sustainable, then there's no more problem with camel.

The Carmody family puts in a major effort every year to keep feral camel populations down. (ABC Landline: Kristy O'Brien)

"Long-term it's better for the country if camel are either cleaned out 100 per cent, or they're commercial and have value."

Camel meat low-allergenic

It has become a win-win situation for Prenti Downs and Albany-based Paul's Pet Foods, with the growing demand for camel meat to manage allergies in pets also contributing to reducing feral camel numbers.

Cattle and feral camels compete for water and vegetation. (Supplied: Mundrabilla Station)

Paul's Pet Foods's Ethan Sylvester said his visit to Prenti Downs was his "most successful" camel cull yet, yielding 77 animals.

His production has increased by 20 per cent each year since 2022, when Mr Sylvester first took his mobile slaughter plant on the 3,000-kilometre return journey, to now culling up to 250 camels per year.

"Kangaroo is still top of the list, but camel has pretty much overtaken beef. It's doing incredibly well … it's growing more and more," Mr Sylvester said.

He said an increasing number of customers were requesting camel meat to help manage skin allergies in their dogs.

Ethan Sylvester harvests feral camels at Prenti Downs Station. (Supplied)

"It's organic, it has no farm contact in the sense of fertilisers and chemicals and drenches," he said.

"It's a really good low-allergen product. As long as people are slowly introducing it to their dogs, they seem to be doing really well."

Paul's Pet Food sources meat directly from Prenti Downs Station. (Supplied: Paul's Pet Foods)

Dietary changes to wild harvest camel

Albany dog owner Jodie Muir Mahuika Fitzpatrick says her two-year-old South African mastiff, Hades, has struggled with skin irritations since he was a puppy.

"He had red rash, skin flare-ups and looked like acne around his mouth and paws," Ms Fitzpatrick said.

"We tried steroids and medicated washes and thousands of dollars at vets and he was just in pain and sore."

Jodie Muir Mahuika Fitzpatrick said Hades's health issues declined after switching to camel meat. (Supplied: Jodie Muir Mahuika Fitzpatrick)

Veterinarian Shey Rogers recommended a diet change to camel meat, which Hades has been eating exclusively for the past six weeks.

"Now he doesn't have any red rash or and hive-like bumps and his coat is shiny and clear and he looks stunning," she said.

Dr Rogers said she saw a lot of dogs with itching or skin issues.

"To try and work out the source of the inflammation, we often recommend they change to a diet they haven't been exposed to before. For a novel diet in pets, we'll often recommend camel," she said.

A novel diet is a meat or protein source that has never been eaten by that dog before, used by veterinarians as a diagnostic tool to pinpoint what a dog's immune system is reacting to.

Game meat is a popular pet food and may be recommended by vets to help diagnose and treat allergies. (ABC Everyday: Ellie Honeybone)

"Once they've finished that diet for six weeks, we can reintroduce one thing into their diet at a time so we can figure out what flares their skin up," Dr Rogers said.

"I'm finding really good feedback from these clients with dogs on the camel diet.

"If we're helping solve a feral camel problem and making use of that meat, I think it's fantastic."

World.title: Beekeepers urge growers to add pollination services to their business plan
World.content:
The Australian horticulture industry has for generations relied on millions of feral honey bees to pollinate crops.

But as varroa mite spreads further north in Queensland, experts say free pollination from wild bee populations is disappearing, forcing growers to rethink how they produce food and secure commercial pollination services.

Bees provide essential pollination services in the horticulture industry. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

North Queensland commercial beekeeper Keith Lang said pollination services could no longer be taken for granted.

"People think bees are all about honey, but we can do without honey," he said.

"We can't do without pollination."

A hidden workforce

The Australian Honey Bee Industry Council says honey bees contribute about $4.6 billion in pollination services each year, helping produce about 65 horticultural crops across the country.

Chief executive Danny Le Feuvre said once varroa mite became established overseas, about 95 per cent of feral honey bee colonies disappeared.

Danny Le Feuvre says growers need to prepare for a reduction in feral bee populations. (ABC News: Tayla Larsen)

"For a long time, growers have benefited from free pollination from feral bees," he said.

"As those populations decline, growers will increasingly rely on managed hives supplied by commercial beekeepers."

The transition comes at a difficult time for the beekeeping industry.

Managing varroa mite has significantly increased costs and labour requirements, while low honey prices have made it harder for many businesses to remain profitable.

Mr Le Feuvre said surveys indicated a significant number of commercial beekeepers were considering leaving the industry just as demand for managed pollination services was expected to rise.

Test kits are used by commercial beekeepers such as Keith Lang to see if they have any varroa mite present in their hives. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

"We know we're going to need more colonies for pollination, but we're losing hives at exactly the same time," he said.

The industry has also released a new national Research, Development and Extension (RD & E) Plan, aimed at strengthening Australia's honey bee and pollination sector as it adapts to varroa mite.

The plan identifies priorities including improving varroa management, accelerating bee breeding and genetics, increasing pollination research, strengthening biosecurity and supporting commercial beekeepers to maintain healthy hive numbers for both honey production and crop pollination.

Beekeepers are struggling to meet demand for hives during pollination season. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

Growers face rising costs

Bundaberg horticultural agronomist and avocado grower Lisa Fyffe knows first-hand how important pollination is for production.

"The European honey bee is definitely the most effective pollinator we have," she said.

"If varroa takes out those wild populations, what do we do then? All of a sudden the reliance on commercial beekeepers increases, and I don't think anyone is really ready for it."

Lisa Fyffe says growers need to work with beekeepers to manage pollination of their crops. (Supplied)

Ms Fyffe said pollination costs had already increased significantly.

"The price has doubled per hive," she said.

"A $50,000 pollination bill suddenly becomes a $100,000 bill. If you don't have the fruit set in the first place, you don't have a crop to sell."

She said growers also needed to rethink how they managed their orchards by providing better habitat for pollinators through flowering ground cover, water sources and improved biodiversity.

"It's so much bigger than what we think," she said.

Planning ahead

The National Farmers' Federation Horticulture Council is encouraging growers to start planning earlier for pollination services rather than waiting until flowering begins.

Executive officer Richard Shannon said growers needed to start treating pollination as an essential business input and incorporate it into their seasonal planning.

Richard Shannon says the costs need to be fairly shared between producers, corporates and consumers. (ABC News: Nathan Morris)

"The purpose is to help growers understand what their future pollination needs might be and encourage them to start those conversations with beekeepers much earlier," he said.

Communication will be critical

Both the horticulture and beekeeping industries agree stronger communication between growers and commercial beekeepers will be essential as Australia continues to adapt to living with varroa mite.

Mr Le Feuvre said early planning was imperative to avoid competition in securing healthy hives for pollination.

He also urged Australians to support local beekeepers by purchasing Australian honey.

"The best way we're going to get through this is by improving profitability for our beekeepers so they can rebuild hive numbers and continue supplying pollination services," he said.

Beekeepers hope their hives are able to survive the varroa mite incursion. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

As the free pollination once provided by feral bees disappears, Keith Lang said commercial beekeepers would carry more of the responsibility for keeping crops productive.

"It's not just beekeepers; it's the farmers as well that's going to be hit," he said.

World.title: Smith says he will '100 per cent' return to PGA Tour if LIV Golf fails
World.content:
Cameron Smith wants LIV Golf to survive, but if it does not, he would "100 per cent" return to the PGA Tour.

"I mean, if it was the only option, I think that's where everyone would want to be for sure, 100 per cent," the Australian and former World No.2 told reporters ahead of this week's LIV Golf New York event. "It would go back to old times."

But Smith made it clear he would strongly prefer that the current times with LIV Golf can continue.

"I want it to work, really, to be honest. It's great fun out here. The team that we've got, I feel like we make each other better, better people and better golfers as well," Smith said. "Yeah, I'd hate to see it go away. We'll see what happens."

Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund announced in April that it will not continue its financial support of the league beyond this season. Smith signed with the breakaway league in 2022, receiving a contract reportedly worth $US140 million ($198.72 million).

Smith is the captain of the all-Australian team Ripper GC.

"What we've been able to do for golf in Australia is really quite important to me, junior golf, the Little Rippers, the event that we have down there, the people it brings out to showcase our great league," Smith said.

"It would be a shame for all that to go away, and I feel like we've worked really hard over the last three or four years to kind of make that all happen."

LIV Golf's Adelaide event in February was among the league's most popular stops this season and set records for golf in Australia. More than 115,000 fans attended across the week in Adelaide, making it the highest-attended golf event in the country's history.

"Australian golf is important to me. I think [LIV] improves it," Smith said.

"I think all the numbers are up. The memberships are up. Social play is up. I think that's in part because of us. So I think it would be a shame for Australian golf if it did go away."

Though multiple reports say the LIV Golf Team Championship scheduled for late August in Michigan will be cancelled amid the league's financial troubles, the players have reportedly been told to prepare as if it is on schedule, and Smith said he's doing just that.

"We had a great year there last year in Detroit, and we're hoping we get back there," he said of the season-ending event from August 27 to 30 at The Cardinal at Saint John's Resort in Plymouth, Michigan.

"It's a great golf course, a great venue, and the crowds really turned up as well. Yeah, would be disappointed if it wasn't."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

LIV Golf has been mum on the status of the $40 million event, which has $11.2 million going to the winning team. However, The Cardinal, which hosted the 2025 LIV team championship, has no tournament infrastructure or fan hospitality built out yet, Front Office Sports reported last week.

Smith said the LIV team is working hard "behind the scenes" to get them playing next year, and he hopes to learn more at an upcoming players' meeting.

"I don't really understand what is going to happen. I think it's all up in the air," he said. "I feel like we're well-informed, but I feel like a lot of it is still up in the air. We don't know."

When asked about his plans if LIV Golf folds, he said he has not made any.

"I'm contracted to the end of next year, so I was expecting to play until the end of next year and renegotiate and hopefully go on," Smith said.

"I'm a positive guy, so I've made no effort to go seek anything else."

Reuters

World.title: Long-awaited corruption report finds firefighter boss exerted extraordinary influence
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaIBAC Long-awaited corruption report finds firefighter boss exerted extraordinary influence Kieran Rooney Updated August 5, 2026 — 9:55am ,first published 9:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An eight-year investigation into negotiations between the Andrews government and the firefighters union has found “serious and concerning conduct” by Victorian ministers, MPs and public servants but stopped short of finding corrupt conduct. The findings were contained in Operation Richmond, an investigation led by the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC) that began in 2018. Operation Richmond centred on dealings between Daniel Andrews’ government and the United Firefighters Union under Peter Marshall. Marija Ercegovac Tabled in parliament on Wednesday after years of delays, IBAC identified serious issues in the way pay deals with the Country Fire Authority (CFA) and the Metropolitan Fire Brigade were negotiated alongside the establishment of Fire Rescue Victoria. “The government placed itself in a position where Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence.” - delayed Operation Richmond report



“IBAC found that senior members of government acted contrary to established policies, procedures, codes of conduct and conventions in negotiating a deal with the secretary of the United Firefighters Union [UFU] , Mr Peter Marshall, for the CFA Enterprise Bargaining Agreement without the knowledge and involvement of the responsible minister, agencies and department,” Commissioner Victoria Elliot said at the start of the report. “By doing so, the government placed itself in a position where Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence over the negotiations for both the CFA EBA and the MFB EBA.” Related Article IBAC Firefighters’ union boss loses court battle to bury corruption investigation, but appeal possible The report covers a period when Daniel Andrews was premier of Victoria. The CFA pay deal became a political flashpoint for his government and the late Jane Garrett resigned as emergency services minister and quit cabinet because she disagreed with her government’s moves to accept UFU demands. “During the period investigated, IBAC also found that

Mr Marshall was afforded privileged access to senior

members of government which, in many cases, were

not disclosed and were to the exclusion of other key

stakeholders,” the report said.



“Operation Richmond highlights how government

leaders, including ministers and the Premier, can

undermine established checks and balances when

they fail to model high integrity standards and act as

stewards of good governance.” The report was initially scheduled for release by the end of June but was delayed by an unsuccessful legal challenge from Marshall. More to come Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Tech industry slams ‘cosmetic’ changes to news levy, US renews ‘extortion’ claim
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaForeign relations Tech industry slams ‘cosmetic’ changes to news levy, US renews ‘extortion’ claim Michael Koziol August 5, 2026 — 9:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: US industry has slammed “cosmetic” changes to Australia’s plans to force big tech companies to pay for news, while the Trump administration renewed its position that the policy extorts American companies. The Albanese government this week finalised legislation for its News Bargaining Incentive, which aims to raise up to $250 million from tech companies – most of which are US-owned – to pay local media firms for journalism content that appears on social media. Anthony Albanese is set to visit the US in September facing strong pushback to his News Bargaining Incentive legislation. Alex Ellinghausen Changes include narrowing the taxable base to digital advertising revenue earned in Australia, rather than all Australian revenue, but increasing the levy to 2.5 per cent from 2.25 per cent. Companies can offset that rate by striking individual, tax-deductible deals. The levy has also been broadened to include social media platforms TikTok and LinkedIn.



The Trump administration has strongly condemned digital services taxes – mostly in Europe – and the US trade office already had the News Bargaining Incentive on its watchlist. On Wednesday, the US State Department indicated the administration retained concerns about Australia’s policy. “As the White House has stated, President Trump is committed to defending America’s leading technology sector from digital services taxes and other forms of foreign extortion,” it said. “The Trump administration will continue to address these issues with our trading partners.” The Trump administration has attacked the legislation as “extortion”. AP Asked whether the concerns had been raised with Australian diplomats, the department said it did not comment on private conversations or characterise confidential exchanges. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, and Google have so far declined to comment on the latest version of the policy. But their representatives in Washington signalled that the companies remain unhappy and are prepared to fight it using the Trump administration.



The Computer & Communications Industry Association, which counts Meta and Google among its members, said the changes to the tax were “for the most part cosmetic” and “critically, do not alter the discriminatory nature of the proposal”. Related Article Publishing ‘Deeply misled’: Nine says news bargaining plan could cost jobs “Targeting a select few foreign firms, mainly American, to fund Australian News businesses, remains a bad policy that is inconsistent with the Australia-US free trade agreement,” said the organisation’s vice president for digital trade, Jonathan McHale. ”Australia should abandon this misguided approach and if it chooses not to, US authorities should respond vigorously. McHale was a long-time senior official at the US Trade Representative, the office responsible for trade deals and tariffs.



The National Foreign Trade Council, a US industry group with Meta, Google and Microsoft in its membership, said it was disappointed that Australia was sticking with the policy and that it now covered a broader spectrum of US companies. Tiffany Smith, the group’s vice-president for global trade, said the Trump administration was “committed to the fair treatment of American companies abroad”. “We call on the Australian government to reconsider this measure, which adds to a broader deteriorating trend in the tax and investment climate in Australia,” she said. The NFTC is chaired by Susan Schwab, a Republican who served as the US Trade Representative under president George W. Bush. The Trump administration has taken a hard line against countries that place additional tax or regulatory burdens on predominantly American tech companies.



At a hearing on the president’s trade agenda two weeks ago, Senate Finance Committee chairman Mike Crapo, a Republican, condemned “a growing array of discriminatory measures in the form of digital services taxes, online content requirements and data localisation”, saying they targeted US firms and posed a threat to American innovation. Related Article Media & marketing News Corp says plan to make tech giants pay for news has been ‘gutted’ The News Bargaining Incentive is one of several issues that pose a challenge for the new Australian ambassador to the US, Greg Moriarty, as well as the incoming US ambassador to Australia, David Brat, a former Republican congressman set to be confirmed in the diplomatic role this week. Australia was also hit with a new 12.5 per cent tariff due to Canberra’s alleged failure to deal with imports produced with forced labour. On Monday (US time), 25 Democrat-run states lodged a legal challenge to those tariffs at the Court of International Trade. It comes ahead of US visits by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who is expected to go to New York in September and attend the G20 in Miami in December, and Foreign Minister Penny Wong, who is due to attend a G20 meeting in Atlanta in October.



Albanese previously suggested he wouldn’t be swayed by pushback from the White House. “We’re a sovereign nation, and my government will make decisions based upon the Australian national interest,” he said in April. “We do that right across the board.” Meta and Google did not respond to requests for comment. Microsoft, which owns LinkedIn, said it shared the government’s objective of promoting a sustainable news ecosystem and appreciated the consultation. “We remain committed to constructive engagement with government, publishers and industry stakeholders to support high-quality journalism, innovation and economic growth,” it said. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Cross-examination continues of complainant on third day of alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the third day of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

This week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex has heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney on Tuesday. Audrey Richardson

The man, now in his early 40s, gave evidence that Jones also groped him as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls farm. On Tuesday, “J” told the court that Jones had indecently assaulted him at the property after telling him to wear “a robe and nothing else”.

The complainant said he came forward to police after seeing reports about Jones’ arrest in November 2024 because he wanted justice.

“I just want justice for what happened; that’s why I’m here,” he said. “I’m here because it’s the right thing to do and people need me, people need me to do this.”

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box. He will face further cross-examination by Jones’ barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, which started on Tuesday afternoon.

Bashir has asked “J” a series of questions about whether he read media reports containing similar allegations about Jones in 2023 before he spoke to police the following year. He said he did not.

The Crown alleges Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020 and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and Bashir said on Monday that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to Judge Glenn Walsh.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Jean-Claude Perrottet set to appear as inquiry enters eighth day
World.content:
Welcome to the Herald’s live coverage of the ICAC’s Operation Rosny public hearings. We’re half-way through week two, and today we’re expecting to hear from a key person of interest to the inquiry, Jean-Claude Perrottet.

I’m state politics reporter Jessica McSweeney, and along with the Herald’s team of senior writers I’ll be bringing all the latest news as it happens from inside the ICAC.

Before we get to today’s evidence, let’s take a look at what we covered yesterday:

World.title: Long-awaited corruption report finds firefighter boss exerted extraordinary influence
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaIBAC Long-awaited corruption report finds firefighter boss exerted extraordinary influence Kieran Rooney Updated August 5, 2026 — 9:55am ,first published 9:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An eight-year investigation into negotiations between the Andrews government and the firefighters union has found “serious and concerning conduct” by Victorian ministers, MPs and public servants but stopped short of finding corrupt conduct. The findings were contained in Operation Richmond, an investigation led by the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC) that began in 2018. Operation Richmond centred on dealings between Daniel Andrews’ government and the United Firefighters Union under Peter Marshall. Marija Ercegovac Tabled in parliament on Wednesday after years of delays, IBAC identified serious issues in the way pay deals with the Country Fire Authority (CFA) and the Metropolitan Fire Brigade were negotiated alongside the establishment of Fire Rescue Victoria. “The government placed itself in a position where Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence.” - delayed Operation Richmond report



“IBAC found that senior members of government acted contrary to established policies, procedures, codes of conduct and conventions in negotiating a deal with the secretary of the United Firefighters Union [UFU] , Mr Peter Marshall, for the CFA Enterprise Bargaining Agreement without the knowledge and involvement of the responsible minister, agencies and department,” Commissioner Victoria Elliot said at the start of the report. “By doing so, the government placed itself in a position where Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence over the negotiations for both the CFA EBA and the MFB EBA.” Related Article IBAC Firefighters’ union boss loses court battle to bury corruption investigation, but appeal possible The report covers a period when Daniel Andrews was premier of Victoria. The CFA pay deal became a political flashpoint for his government and the late Jane Garrett resigned as emergency services minister and quit cabinet because she disagreed with her government’s moves to accept UFU demands. “During the period investigated, IBAC also found that

Mr Marshall was afforded privileged access to senior

members of government which, in many cases, were

not disclosed and were to the exclusion of other key

stakeholders,” the report said.



“Operation Richmond highlights how government

leaders, including ministers and the Premier, can

undermine established checks and balances when

they fail to model high integrity standards and act as

stewards of good governance.” The report was initially scheduled for release by the end of June but was delayed by an unsuccessful legal challenge from Marshall. More to come Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Tech industry slams ‘cosmetic’ changes to news levy, US renews ‘extortion’ claim
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaForeign relations Tech industry slams ‘cosmetic’ changes to news levy, US renews ‘extortion’ claim Michael Koziol August 5, 2026 — 9:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: US industry has slammed “cosmetic” changes to Australia’s plans to force big tech companies to pay for news, while the Trump administration renewed its position that the policy extorts American companies. The Albanese government this week finalised legislation for its News Bargaining Incentive, which aims to raise up to $250 million from tech companies – most of which are US-owned – to pay local media firms for journalism content that appears on social media. Anthony Albanese is set to visit the US in September facing strong pushback to his News Bargaining Incentive legislation. Alex Ellinghausen Changes include narrowing the taxable base to digital advertising revenue earned in Australia, rather than all Australian revenue, but increasing the levy to 2.5 per cent from 2.25 per cent. Companies can offset that rate by striking individual, tax-deductible deals. The levy has also been broadened to include social media platforms TikTok and LinkedIn.



The Trump administration has strongly condemned digital services taxes – mostly in Europe – and the US trade office already had the News Bargaining Incentive on its watchlist. On Wednesday, the US State Department indicated the administration retained concerns about Australia’s policy. “As the White House has stated, President Trump is committed to defending America’s leading technology sector from digital services taxes and other forms of foreign extortion,” it said. “The Trump administration will continue to address these issues with our trading partners.” The Trump administration has attacked the legislation as “extortion”. AP Asked whether the concerns had been raised with Australian diplomats, the department said it did not comment on private conversations or characterise confidential exchanges. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, and Google have so far declined to comment on the latest version of the policy. But their representatives in Washington signalled that the companies remain unhappy and are prepared to fight it using the Trump administration.



The Computer & Communications Industry Association, which counts Meta and Google among its members, said the changes to the tax were “for the most part cosmetic” and “critically, do not alter the discriminatory nature of the proposal”. Related Article Publishing ‘Deeply misled’: Nine says news bargaining plan could cost jobs “Targeting a select few foreign firms, mainly American, to fund Australian News businesses, remains a bad policy that is inconsistent with the Australia-US free trade agreement,” said the organisation’s vice president for digital trade, Jonathan McHale. ”Australia should abandon this misguided approach and if it chooses not to, US authorities should respond vigorously. McHale was a long-time senior official at the US Trade Representative, the office responsible for trade deals and tariffs.



The National Foreign Trade Council, a US industry group with Meta, Google and Microsoft in its membership, said it was disappointed that Australia was sticking with the policy and that it now covered a broader spectrum of US companies. Tiffany Smith, the group’s vice-president for global trade, said the Trump administration was “committed to the fair treatment of American companies abroad”. “We call on the Australian government to reconsider this measure, which adds to a broader deteriorating trend in the tax and investment climate in Australia,” she said. The NFTC is chaired by Susan Schwab, a Republican who served as the US Trade Representative under president George W. Bush. The Trump administration has taken a hard line against countries that place additional tax or regulatory burdens on predominantly American tech companies.



At a hearing on the president’s trade agenda two weeks ago, Senate Finance Committee chairman Mike Crapo, a Republican, condemned “a growing array of discriminatory measures in the form of digital services taxes, online content requirements and data localisation”, saying they targeted US firms and posed a threat to American innovation. Related Article Media & marketing News Corp says plan to make tech giants pay for news has been ‘gutted’ The News Bargaining Incentive is one of several issues that pose a challenge for the new Australian ambassador to the US, Greg Moriarty, as well as the incoming US ambassador to Australia, David Brat, a former Republican congressman set to be confirmed in the diplomatic role this week. Australia was also hit with a new 12.5 per cent tariff due to Canberra’s alleged failure to deal with imports produced with forced labour. On Monday (US time), 25 Democrat-run states lodged a legal challenge to those tariffs at the Court of International Trade. It comes ahead of US visits by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who is expected to go to New York in September and attend the G20 in Miami in December, and Foreign Minister Penny Wong, who is due to attend a G20 meeting in Atlanta in October.



Albanese previously suggested he wouldn’t be swayed by pushback from the White House. “We’re a sovereign nation, and my government will make decisions based upon the Australian national interest,” he said in April. “We do that right across the board.” Meta and Google did not respond to requests for comment. Microsoft, which owns LinkedIn, said it shared the government’s objective of promoting a sustainable news ecosystem and appreciated the consultation. “We remain committed to constructive engagement with government, publishers and industry stakeholders to support high-quality journalism, innovation and economic growth,” it said. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Cross-examination continues of complainant on third day of alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the third day of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

This week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex has heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney on Tuesday. Audrey Richardson

The man, now in his early 40s, gave evidence that Jones also groped him as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls farm. On Tuesday, “J” told the court that Jones had indecently assaulted him at the property after telling him to wear “a robe and nothing else”.

The complainant said he came forward to police after seeing reports about Jones’ arrest in November 2024 because he wanted justice.

“I just want justice for what happened; that’s why I’m here,” he said. “I’m here because it’s the right thing to do and people need me, people need me to do this.”

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box. He will face further cross-examination by Jones’ barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, which started on Tuesday afternoon.

Bashir has asked “J” a series of questions about whether he read media reports containing similar allegations about Jones in 2023 before he spoke to police the following year. He said he did not.

The Crown alleges Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020 and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and Bashir said on Monday that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to Judge Glenn Walsh.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.
